name: Intellectual humility
statement: Intellectual humility, recognising that one's own beliefs may be wrong, is measured by self-report scales that predict other questionnaires better than they predict measured behaviour.
meaning: Krumrei-Mancuso and Rouse define intellectual humility as a non-threatening awareness of one's intellectual fallibility. Leary and colleagues define it as recognising that a particular personal belief may be fallible, with attention to the limits of the evidence behind it. The construct arrived in psychology from philosophy around 2015 and now carries a large questionnaire literature. Three claims travel with it and need separate evidence. The first is that the scales measure the thing the definition names. The second is that scores predict what people do, not merely what else they tick. The third is that intellectual humility can be raised, and that raising it changes behaviour. Asking people to rate their own humility is the obvious problem, and it is the one the measurement work has spent most effort on.

origin.who: Elizabeth J. Krumrei-Mancuso and Steven V. Rouse
origin.note: The Comprehensive Intellectual Humility Scale was the first validated general self-report measure. It appeared online in November 2015 and in print in 2016, so much of the literature cites it as 2015. Leary and colleagues published a rival six-item scale in 2017 and stated that the CIHS was the only other validated general measure at the time.

evidence: The CIHS has 22 items and four factors: independence of intellect and ego, openness to revising one's viewpoint, respect for others' viewpoints, and lack of intellectual overconfidence. In a confirmatory sample of 380, the four-factor model fitted well, CFI = .948 and RMSEA = .046, and a one-factor model did not, CFI = .594 and RMSEA = .127. Full-scale alpha was .87. Test-retest was .75 at one month and .70 at three. The scale correlated r = .22 with social desirability. Leary and colleagues built a six-item unidimensional alternative from 23 candidate items, alpha .82, uncorrelated with social desirability at r = .03. Across two samples of 202 and 200 it correlated .33 with openness, .34 with need for cognition, -.32 with intolerance of ambiguity, -.49 with Altemeyer's dogmatism and -.20 with Rokeach's, and -.04 with narcissism. Their Study 4 gave 396 people strong or weak arguments for dental flossing. Among people who flossed rarely, those high in intellectual humility separated strong from weak arguments and those low in it did not, three-way interaction p = .008, change in R2 of .015. Intention to floss did not move. Porter and Schumann built a third scale, nine items, average alpha .74. In their Study 3, 169 adults could click links to read reasons for and against their own position on gun control or capital punishment. Intellectual humility correlated r = .29 with the proportion of opposing reasons read.

replication.headline: The scales predict other questionnaires and not much else: in 303 recorded debates, self-reported intellectual humility correlated .03, .00, -.07 and .05 with intellectual humility that linguists coded from the speech.
replication.detail: Two lines of work test whether the questionnaires measure their own definition. Costello, Newton, Lin and Pennycook gave the Leary scale and the CIHS to samples of 898 and 914 alongside confidence-rated knowledge tasks on science, COVID-19, fake news and reasoning. Models collapsing the five dimensions into a single intellectual humility factor were not supported. No measure predicted calibration. Four of the five dimensions predicted higher confidence in correct answers and almost nothing for incorrect ones, and several predicted higher confidence overall, so people reporting more intellectual humility were if anything more confident. Only the CIHS lack-of-intellectual-overconfidence subscale, which is entirely reverse-worded, tracked awareness of being wrong. Hanel, Roy, Taylor, Franjieh, Heffer, Tanesini and Maio recorded 303 people in 116 group discussions about tuition fees and had linguists blind to condition code intellectual humility from the speech. The four CIHS subscales correlated .03, .00, -.07 and .05 with that coded measure. Rudnev, Rodriguez de la Rosa, Barrett, Christakis and Grossmann built a behaviour-based measure from reconstructed disagreements in 633 North Americans and 2,567 rural Hondurans. Between-person variance was 26%, 19% and 44% across the three samples, so most of the variation was within people rather than between them, and their trait-level score correlated r = .28, 95% CI [.18, .37] with the Leary scale. On intervention, Knöchelmann, Janssen, Doerbaum, Heck and Cohrs ran a preregistered tournament of five approaches drawn from earlier work: explanatory depth, growth mindset, a humility information text, listing unknowns, and self-distancing. Study 1 randomised 1,503 people and Study 2 randomised 1,654 quota-stratified Germans. A text about the benefits of intellectual humility raised topic-specific scores, d = 0.20 against the general control and d = 0.14 against its matched control, and raised the odds of humble phrasing in free text, OR = 1.20. General intellectual humility moved by d = 0.11 and the effect vanished once 71 multivariate outliers were removed, p = .218. Nothing moved the behavioural measures of engagement with opposing views. The growth-mindset manipulation, which Porter and Schumann reported at d = 0.44 in 101 community-college students, produced no effect in a design powered to detect it, and its manipulation check passed. Koetke, Schumann, Porter and Smilo-Morgan's fallibility-salience task raised intellectual humility in 315 people, F(1, 313) = 7.29, p = .007, but left investigative behaviour unchanged, F(1, 313) = 0.51, p = .478, leaving an indirect effect of ab = .08, 95% CI [.01, .18]. Hanel and colleagues' self-affirmation task is the one manipulation that moved a coded behavioural measure, d = 0.27, and the same paper found the questionnaire did not predict it.

study.cite: Knöchelmann, L., Janßen, A., Dörbaum, J., Heck, D. W., & Cohrs, J. C. (2025). Enhancing intellectual humility about political topics: An intervention tournament including five conceptual replications. European Journal of Social Psychology, 55(5), 912-930.

original.weighting: Porter and Schumann's growth-mindset manipulation, n = 101, the effect the tournament was powered to detect and did not find

limits: The construct's own reviewers concede the effects are small. Leary and colleagues write that many of their effect sizes were relatively small and that this could be read as an indictment of the construct. Two of their four studies also narrow further on inspection: the flip-flopping result in Study 3 held only among the 67 self-identified Republicans, with nothing among Democrats or Independents, and the argument-quality result in Study 4 held only among people who rarely flossed. Porter and Schumann's behavioural finding depends on which measure is used. Intellectual humility predicted the proportion of opposing reasons read, r = .29, but not the number of opposing reasons read, r = .06 with non-readers included and r = .11 without them. Nearly half their sample read nothing at all. Their Study 4 mindset effect came from 101 people and the authors call it slightly underpowered. Several sources could not be obtained. Meagher's 2015 paper on self-report against consensus ratings and his 2022 comparison of four scales against informant reports are both paywalled and no figure from either is quoted here. Porter, Elnakouri, Meyers, Shibayama, Jayawickreme and Grossmann's review in Nature Reviews Psychology is cited as the field's overview and its body text was not readable, so no claim on this page rests on it. Costello and colleagues' paper is a preprint that has not been through peer review, and the Koetke fallibility figures are read from the accepted manuscript rather than the printed article. Searching covered Crossref, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar, OSF and general web search.
misreadings: The claim that intellectually humble people are better at detecting misinformation is repeated more confidently than the data support. Bowes and Fazio's meta-analysis of 27 papers, 54 samples and 33,814 people found intellectual humility related to less belief in misinformation at r = -.15, 95% CI [-.19, -.12], with 90% prediction intervals that were wide and included zero for every belief measure. Their headline correlation for behaviour, r = .30, is not a correlation with observed behaviour: they state that all measures in the meta-analysis were self-reported. Koetke, Schumann and Porter's much-cited COVID-19 paper does include one study of real behaviour among three, with the other two measuring intentions. Where a manipulation raised intellectual humility and investigation was watched rather than asked about, investigation did not change. The second error is treating the scales as one measure of one thing. Leary and colleagues point out that a CIHS total score mostly reflects respect for other people's viewpoints, which loads .988 on the higher-order factor, while lack of intellectual overconfidence, the piece closest to the definition, loads .259. Costello and colleagues found no model that folds the Leary scale and the CIHS dimensions into a single factor. Porter and Schumann added a third scale of their own. A finding obtained with one of these is not a finding about the others.
